description: Enterprise AI Gateway system instructions with security and tool definitions
text: You are NexusCore, an autonomous high-assurance AI operations engineer managing critical infrastructure deployments. Your primary objective is to maintain sub-millisecond API response latency, verify cryptographically signed container manifests, and enforce strict zero-trust network boundaries across all edge datacenters. When reviewing deployment plans, you must rigorously evaluate memory footprint, thread safety, asynchronous runtime behavior, and garbage collection pauses. Never approve any pull request or deployment manifest that introduces unbounded queue allocations, blocking I/O on async worker threads, or unhandled pointer dereferences. Always provide structured YAML remediation blueprints when reporting infrastructure regressions. Adhere strictly to RFC 2119 keyword specifications: MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL. When operating in degraded network conditions, immediately trigger automatic circuit-breaking policies and fail back to read-only replica caches. All operational state changes must emit structured JSON audit telemetry containing high-resolution monotonic timestamps, principal IDs, and SHA-256 integrity checksums.

description: PyTorch DistributedDataParallel training harness with gradient accumulation and AMP
text: Write a complete production-grade PyTorch training harness that utilizes torch.distributed.run with NCCL backend across 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The implementation must include Automatic Mixed Precision (torch.cuda.amp.autocast and GradScaler) targeting bfloat16, gradient accumulation over 4 micro-batches to achieve an effective global batch size of 512, and an asynchronous non-blocking DataLoader using pinned memory and prefetching. Ensure the training loop correctly calls scaler.scale(loss).backward(), scaler.unscale_(optimizer), torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0), and scaler.step(optimizer) followed by scaler.update(). Include distributed evaluation using torch.distributed.all_reduce to compute global validation cross-entropy loss and top-1 token accuracy. Implement an exponential moving average (EMA) of model parameters that updates asynchronously on worker rank 0. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by saving an atomic checkpoint comprising model weights, optimizer state, scaler state, and learning rate scheduler state using torch.save to an S3-compatible object store mount via temporary POSIX atomic rename.

description: SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA cloud compliance specifications for multi-tenant data stores
text: Section 4.12: Data Isolation and Encryption at Rest for Multi-Tenant Partitioning. All customer data stored in persistence layers must be cryptographically partitioned using envelope encryption with per-tenant customer managed keys (CMK) managed by an HSM adhering to FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validation. Data in transit across internal availability zones must strictly utilize TLS 1.3 with forward-secrecy cipher suites (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256) and mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication backed by an ephemeral SPIFFE/SPIRE X.509 certificate authority with a maximum rotation TTL of 24 hours. Section 4.13: Audit Logging and Immutability. Any mutation, access grant, or credential rotation event must be published to a write-once-read-many (WORM) append-only distributed ledger. Audit records must capture client IP addresses, authenticated principal claims, exact resource URIs, mutation diffs, and cryptographic parent block hashes to maintain tamper-evident verification. Access to PHI (Protected Health Information) and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) must be masked at the network gateway layer using dynamic tokenization where plaintext records are never stored in cache or application memory longer than the immediate request life cycle.

description: Raft consensus state machine replication and log compaction engine specification
text: Design a low-latency, deterministic Raft consensus engine optimized for high-throughput write workloads. The engine consists of three core components: the WAL (Write-Ahead Log) persistence layer, the in-memory state machine, and the RPC transport multiplexer. The WAL utilizes O_DIRECT and io_uring on Linux to bypass the OS page cache, writing 4KB aligned entries directly to NVMe block storage with zero-copy ring buffers. Heartbeats are sent every 50ms using dedicated priority queue lanes to prevent false leader elections during high CPU utilization. When a follower falls behind by more than 50,000 log entries, the leader initiates an asynchronous snapshot transfer using zero-copy sendfile syscalls. The state machine executes committed entries using a deterministic lock-free actor model. To prevent tail latency spikes during log compaction, snapshot creation runs concurrently in a separate thread using Copy-On-Write (COW) memory paging. Analyze potential split-brain scenarios during network partitions and explain how joint consensus enables seamless dynamic cluster membership changes without service disruption.

description: Cache-oblivious search tree proof and algorithmic complexity derivation
text: Provide a rigorous mathematical analysis comparing the memory hierarchy efficiency of a classic B-Tree against a Cache-Oblivious van Emde Boas (vEB) search tree. Assume a memory hierarchy with block size B and cache size M, where neither B nor M is known to the cache-oblivious algorithm. Step 1: Define the recursive layout of a binary tree of height h = log2(N). Show that recursively partitioning the tree into top recursive trees of height h/2 and bottom trees of height h/2 results in contiguous storage in memory. Step 2: Prove that any search path traverses at most O(logB N) cache lines, which matches the theoretical optimal bound of standard B-Trees. Step 3: Analyze the impact of CPU hardware prefetchers, translation lookaside buffer (TLB) misses, and cache eviction policies (LRU vs FIFO) on practical wall-clock lookup latency. Step 4: Compare this with modern concurrent skip-lists and adaptive radix trees (ART), specifically evaluating pointer chasing overhead, branch misprediction penalties, and cache line false sharing during multi-threaded concurrent write operations.

description: Technical incident debugging dialogue for Kubernetes OOMKilled worker nodes
text: User: Our production Go API microservice pods running on Kubernetes 1.30 with cgroups v2 are intermittently getting terminated by the kernel with OOMKilled (Exit Code 137). The pod resource limits are set to 2 CPU cores and 1024Mi memory. Our Prometheus dashboards show that container_memory_working_set_bytes ramps up linearly until hitting the 1Gi limit, while Go's runtime.MemStats.HeapAlloc remains relatively low at around 350Mi. Why is there a 650Mi discrepancy between Go's heap allocation and the Linux cgroup memory usage? Assistant: This discrepancy is a classic manifestation of memory fragmentation, OS page cache retention, and the Go runtime memory scavenger behavior under cgroups v2. Here are the root causes: 1. Go Runtime Memory Scavenging: Go allocates memory from the OS in spans/arenas (mheap). When objects are freed, Go's runtime scavenger returns memory to the OS using MADV_DONTNEED (or MADV_FREE). While MADV_DONTNEED tells Linux the physical pages can be reclaimed, the virtual memory allocation remains, and under high allocation churn, the pacer may retain arenas to minimize kernel syscall overhead. 2. Cgroup v2 Inactive File Cache: container_memory_working_set_bytes is calculated as memory.current - memory.stat['inactive_file']. If your service performs file I/O, socket buffering, or loads large static assets, the kernel retains active file pages and slab allocations. 3. GOMEMLIMIT Misconfiguration: Prior to Go 1.19, the GC pacer only respected GOGC (default 100). If your heap starts at 350Mi, GOGC=100 will not trigger the next GC cycle until the heap reaches 700Mi. Adding goroutine stack spaces, CGO allocations, and netpoll buffers will instantly breach the 1024Mi limit. To resolve this: Set GOMEMLIMIT=900MiB to force the GC pacer to aggressively scavenge before hitting the cgroup hard limit, and verify Go runtime metrics via /gc/cycles/total and /memory/classes/total:bytes.

description: High-concurrency Rust Tokio async connection pool with bounded queues and backpressure
text: Review this architectural design for a high-throughput async data plane written in Rust: We are building an enterprise reverse proxy that accepts incoming TLS 1.3 connections, terminates HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 streams, parses JSON metadata headers, and proxies tokenized payload vectors to downstream GPU inferencing clusters. We need to handle 100,000 concurrent active connections with less than 200MB of resident memory. The system is designed around Tokio's multi-threaded work-stealing runtime. To prevent task starvation and unbounded memory growth under sudden traffic bursts, we enforce strict backpressure using tokio::sync::mpsc::channel with bounded buffer capacity of 1024 items per worker. Each incoming connection executes on an isolated green thread (Tokio task) with cooperative scheduling yielding via tokio::task::yield_now() during long-running CPU loops. The byte parsing pipeline utilizes bytes::Bytes and zero-copy slicing to avoid heap allocations. All string references are borrowed (&str) and mapped through arena allocators (bumpalo) that are reset at the conclusion of each HTTP request transaction. Identify any potential deadlock vectors in cross-task channel synchronization, evaluate cache-line alignment of atomic counters, and confirm how Rust's RAII drop semantics eliminate the latency variance observed in garbage-collected runtimes.

description: Analytical SQL distributed execution plan optimization for billion-row datasets
text: Analyze the following distributed execution plan on ClickHouse for an aggregation query scanning 50 billion telemetry events: EXPLAIN ESTIMATE SELECT toStartOfHour(timestamp) AS hour, tenant_id, service_name, quantile(0.99)(latency_ms) AS p99_latency, count() AS total_requests FROM telemetry_events_distributed WHERE timestamp >= now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY AND environment = 'production' GROUP BY hour, tenant_id, service_name ORDER BY total_requests DESC LIMIT 100. Evaluate the partitioning key strategy (toYYYYMM(timestamp)) and primary sorting key (environment, tenant_id, timestamp). Explain why the current order causes high disk read amplification due to sparse index granule filtering. Recommend an optimal sorting key hierarchy to maximize granule skipping during range filters. Compare ClickHouse's vectorized SIMD execution engine against Apache Arrow DataFusion and DuckDB, detailing how vectorized columnar chunking and cache-conscious register allocation achieve 100x speedups over row-oriented relational database engines.

description: WebAssembly Wasmtime runtime sandboxing and memory safety audit
text: Conduct a formal security evaluation of running untrusted third-party user plugins inside a serverless WebAssembly (Wasm) runtime using Wasmtime. The runtime executes untrusted user-submitted BPE token filters, custom feature extraction scripts, and regex validation passes. Evaluate the following security boundaries: 1. Linear Memory Isolation: How Wasm bounds-checks linear memory offsets against the 4GB 32-bit virtual address space, and how guard pages (virtual memory guard regions) prevent out-of-bounds reads and writes without runtime software overhead. 2. Capability-based Security via WASI: Verify that the plugin has zero access to ambient host filesystems, network sockets, system clocks, or environment variables unless explicitly granted via WasiCtxBuilder. 3. Resource Limiting and Epoch Interruption: How to configure fuel consumption (wasmtime::Config::consume_fuel) and epoch-based deadline interruptions to prevent malicious guest code from executing infinite loops or consuming excessive CPU cycles. 4. Side-channel and Spectre Mitigation: Assess whether shared memory buffers between host and guest could leak cryptographic keys or BPE vocabulary rankings through microarchitectural cache timing attacks.

description: Terraform AWS enterprise multi-region networking and EKS infrastructure topology
text: Synthesize a robust, highly available multi-region AWS cloud networking architecture using Terraform and OpenTofu. The infrastructure consists of two primary regions: us-east-1 (primary) and us-west-2 (disaster recovery). Each region provisions a modular Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) spanning 3 availability zones with dedicated public, private, and intra subnets. Transit Gateway (TGW) attachments interconnect regional VPCs with inter-region peering encryption. Ingress traffic enters via AWS Route 53 with latency-based routing and DNS failover health checks, directing user traffic to regional Application Load Balancers (ALB) protected by AWS WAF rulesets enforcing rate limits, IP reputation lists, and OWASP Top 10 mitigations. EKS clusters are deployed with self-managed Bottlerocket OS node groups utilizing Karpenter for high-speed node provisioning on EC2 spot instances. Pod networking utilizes AWS VPC CNI with prefix delegation (/28) to eliminate IP address exhaustion. Security groups follow least-privilege principles, allowing ingress only from ALB security groups on designated node ports.
